PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al                 )        Docket Nos. EL25-49-000
                                                   )                    EL25-49-001

v.                                                 )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                        )        (Consolidated)


                       RESPONSE OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)1, the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”), respectfully

submits this Response to the February 23, 2026 Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

(“PJM”)2 and the February 23, 2026 Initial Brief of the PJM Transmission Owners (“TOs”)3 in

this Order to Show Cause Proceeding.


    I.   Introduction

         DCC appreciates the Commission’s leadership in initiating this proceeding and its

recognition that existing transmission service frameworks are not well-suited to accommodate

the rapid growth of large, co-located loads. The Commission’s directive to develop new

transmission service constructs reflects a thoughtful and innovative effort to modernize




1
  18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
  Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49-000 (Feb. 23, 2026) (“PJM Initial Brief”).
3
  Initial Brief and Joint Responses of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Docket No. EL25-49-000 (Feb. 23,
2026) (“TOs Initial Brief”).

                                                       1
 transmission policy in a manner that supports reliability, affordability, and economic

development.

        DCC supports the Commission’s objective of enabling new large loads to interconnect in

a timely and efficient manner, including through arrangements that pair load with generation

resources. Co-location is not the only pathway to achieve these goals, but it is an important and

promising one that can provide system benefits, including more efficient siting, potential

reductions in transmission impacts — such as avoided or deferred transmission buildout, reduced

congestion, and associated system cost savings — and alignment with broader federal and state

policy objectives encouraging coordinated development of load and generation.

        However, as the Commission has recognized, the success of these new service constructs

depends on their implementation. While PJM and the TOs have proposed frameworks intended

to comply with the Commission’s directives, DCC is concerned that, as currently structured,

these proposals will not enable commercially viable arrangements. Instead, the proposals

introduce significant operational rigidity, limit flexibility, and create disincentives that will

impede the development of co-located load and associated generation. This is fundamentally at

odds with the Commission’s December directive.

        DCC respectfully submits that targeted modifications are necessary to ensure that the

framework ultimately adopted by the Commission is workable, flexible, and aligned with the

Commission’s stated objectives.


 II.    PJM’s Clarifications Confirm that the Proposed Framework Does Not Preserve the
        Core Value Proposition of Co-Location

        DCC appreciates PJM’s recent stakeholder engagement and efforts to clarify the intended

operation of the proposed service constructs, including through its March 16, 2026 workshop



                                                   2
 materials.4 These materials provide important insight into how PJM intends to operationalize

Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS”) and Contract Demand

Transmission Services.

        In particular, PJM confirms that, under Interim NITS, co-located load “will not have

rights to the capacity/energy from any specific co-located generation” and that such generation is

treated as part of the “network” resource pool rather than as a dedicated supply resource for the

co-located load.5 PJM further explains that, while it would endeavor to dispatch co-located

generation to reduce curtailment risk, such dispatch would not eliminate that risk.

        From a customer perspective, the fundamental reason to pursue co-location is to achieve

speed to energization and greater operational predictability by pairing load with generation.

However, under PJM’s proposed framework, even a customer that brings sufficient co-located

generation to meet its load cannot avoid curtailment risk. If co-location does not provide any

meaningful ability to mitigate curtailment or ensure more predictable service, it is unclear why a

customer would pursue this pathway at all.

        This raises a fundamental question as to whether PJM’s proposal reflects the outcome the

Commission intended in establishing Interim NITS. The Commission’s objective was to enable

more flexible and timely service arrangements for co-located load. PJM’s proposed framework

in which customers may still be curtailed despite bringing their own generation does not appear

to align with that objective.

        PJM’s March 16 clarification confirms that, under the proposed framework, co-location

does not provide any assured or priority access to on-site generation for load taking Interim



4
  PJM, Co-Located Load Use Cases Presentation at 12 (Mar. 16, 2026), available at 20260316-item-02---co-
located-load-use-cases---presentation.pdf
5
  Id.

                                                      3
 NITS. Instead, both load and generation are fully integrated into the network construct, and the

linkage between the two is effectively severed.6 Further, the proposal does not even recognize an

intermediate operational state in which co-located generation can operate in parallel with the grid

on a limited, non-exporting or non-market-participating basis while completing interconnection

requirements. Instead, generation is effectively treated as either fully integrated into PJM’s

network construct or not available at all.

           If a customer that develops or procures on-site generation cannot rely on that generation

to serve its load or aid in avoiding curtailment with any degree of predictability, co-location loses

its functional meaning and appeal. The Commission should therefore require PJM to modify its

proposal to ensure that co-located generation provides meaningful and predictable service to the

co-located load that enabled its development by ensuring that new co-located generation confers

curtailment protection to its associated load—up to its output—except under system emergency

conditions requiring manual load shed (e.g., EEA Level 3).


III.       The Proposal Unnecessarily Restricts the Use of Non-Firm Service and Precludes
           Incremental Solutions

           DCC is also concerned that PJM’s proposed limitations on Non-Firm Contract Demand

Service (“Non-Firm CDS”) create an artificial barrier to incremental and timely service. PJM’s

stakeholder materials confirm that Non-Firm CDS is limited to use when the co-located

generator is unavailable and must be requested in advance, with load consumption from the grid

limited to approved firm and non-firm service levels.7 PJM further illustrates that where a

customer is not granted the full amount of requested firm service due to transmission constraints,




6
    Id.
7
    PJM, Co-Located Load Use Cases Presentation at 5, 7 (Mar. 16, 2026).

                                                         4
 the customer is not permitted to use additional Non-Firm CDS to serve the remaining load until

upgrades are complete.8

           DCC recognizes that PJM views Non-Firm CDS as a limited, backup product and

emphasizes reliability considerations in constraining its use. However, PJM has not

demonstrated why Non-Firm service that is (a) requested in advance, (b) subject to PJM

approval, (c) fully curtailable, and (d) supported by required protection and control mechanisms,

may appropriately be used to address generator outages but may not be used to address

temporary transmission constraints. This restrictive interpretation is inconsistent with the

Commission’s directives in the Show Cause Order. In Paragraphs 214 and 215, the Commission

established Non-Firm Contract Demand service as a flexible, as-available transmission product

that may be used “from time to time when transmission capacity is available” and “as needed

during normal, non-emergency system operating conditions.” The Commission further required

that this service “must be available during normal operations,” subject to curtailment when

necessary.9

           While the Commission provided generator outage as an example use case, it did not limit

the service to that circumstance. To the contrary, the Commission’s plain language contemplates

broader availability whenever excess transmission capacity exists and reliability can be

maintained. By contrast, PJM’s proposal effectively confines Non-Firm CDS to a narrow,

outage-only function and prohibits its use to address foreseeable and manageable transmission

constraints. This limitation is not supported by the Order and improperly narrows a Commission-

directed service designed to provide flexible, incremental access to the transmission system.




8
    Id. at 11.
9
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at 214–215 (2025).

                                                        5
        As a result, PJM’s proposal does not merely interpret the Commission’s directive—it

materially narrows it. By constraining Non-Firm CDS to a limited outage-only function, PJM

eliminates the very flexibility the Commission sought to introduce. This approach prevents

customers from utilizing available transmission capacity to serve load on a conditional, as-

available basis and instead forces an “all-or-nothing” framework in which load cannot be served

until full firm service is available. Such an outcome is inconsistent with commercial realities and

undermines the Commission’s objective of enabling more timely and flexible transmission

service for co-located load.


IV.    The Proposal Does Not Provide a Workable Pathway for Phased Development or
       Load Ramping

       The proposed framework also fails to accommodate the phased and incremental

development that characterizes large load projects. PJM’s proposal requires that gross load and

generation configurations be specified upfront and treats material changes in those

configurations as requiring new applications and studies (see PJM Initial Brief). At the same

time, PJM prohibits the mixing of NITS and Contract Demand Transmission Services for the

same load.

       While PJM has acknowledged limited flexibility in certain circumstances, it does not

provide a clear or workable pathway for customers to (a) ramp load over time, (b) transition

between service constructs, or (c) seek to align transmission service with phased project

development. This lack of clarity is particularly problematic given that data center and other

large load facilities are typically developed in stages. The absence of a defined ramping

framework introduces uncertainty, increases the risk of delay, and may require repeated study

cycles that are not aligned with project timelines. The Commission should require PJM to

establish clear rules and processes that enable incremental load additions without triggering

                                                 6
 unnecessary re-study or requiring customers to fundamentally restructure their service

arrangements.


 V.      Curtailment Risk and Operational Parameters Remain Insufficiently Defined

         PJM’s proposal relies heavily on curtailment as a mechanism to maintain system

reliability, but it does not provide sufficient clarity regarding how curtailment will be applied in

practice. PJM does establish a general curtailment priority among service types. However, the

framework does not clearly define: (a) the operational relationship between co-located load and

co-located generation; (b) the specific conditions under which curtailment will be triggered; (c)

the extent of advance notice that will be provided; (d) the expected duration or frequency of

curtailment events; or (e) how curtailment will be implemented in mixed service configurations.

         Moreover, PJM acknowledges that existing systems do not fully support the granularity

required to implement certain aspects of the proposed services, which may necessitate additional

operational workarounds or infrastructure.10 At the same time, PJM proposes an extremely

stringent penalty framework under which a single failure to comply with load shedding or

curtailment instructions results in automatic disqualification from service.11 This “one-strike”

consequence is particularly concerning in light of the operational ambiguity described above.

         Given the lack of clearly defined curtailment triggers, procedures, and system

implementation details, it is unreasonable to impose such severe penalties for a single non-

compliance event. Customers are being asked to comply with operational requirements that

remain largely undefined, while bearing the full risk of immediate and potentially long-term loss

of service for any failure—an approach that is patently unacceptable and emblematic of PJM’s


10
  PJM Initial Brief at 65–66.
11
  PJM Initial Brief at 41–43 (providing that a single instance of failing to follow curtailment or load shed
procedures results in disqualification).

                                                           7
 broader effort to avoid implementing the Commission’s directive while shifting all compliance

risk onto customers.

       In addition, PJM does not adequately address the extent to which curtailment compliance

may depend on transmission owner facilities, communications systems, or other infrastructure

that is outside the direct control of the load customer. In such circumstances, it is unclear why

the load customer would bear the full consequence of a curtailment failure. Assigning strict, one-

strike liability to customers for failures that may be caused, in whole or in part, by third-party

systems is unjust and unreasonable, and further underscores the inequitable allocation of risk

embedded in PJM’s proposal.

       While DCC recognizes the importance of preserving operator flexibility to maintain

reliability, the combination of undefined operational parameters and severe, strict-liability

penalty provisions creates an unreasonable allocation of risk. Customers cannot reasonably

assess or manage curtailment risk without greater transparency and structure, nor can they be

expected to accept a framework in which a single event—potentially outside their control—

results in loss of service. The Commission should require PJM to provide additional detail and

guardrails to ensure that curtailment operates as a predictable and bounded tool, and that any

associated penalty framework is proportionate, clearly defined, and appropriately allocates

responsibility among relevant parties.


VI.    The Proposal is Materially Incomplete and Relies on Future Developments

       DCC is also concerned that the proposed framework leaves numerous critical elements

undefined or deferred. As described in PJM’s filings, key aspects of the proposal—including

telemetry and metering requirements, tracking of unreserved use, settlement implications, and




                                                  8
  certain penalty provisions—remain under development or are identified as requiring future tariff

 revisions (see PJM Initial Brief).

        A framework that relies on significant future development for core operational and

 financial components raises concerns regarding whether the proposed services are sufficiently

 defined to be found just and reasonable at this stage. The Commission should ensure that the

 essential elements of the proposed services are clearly specified and operationally feasible prior

 to approval.


VII.    The Proposed Implementation Timeline Warrants Refinement

        PJM proposes an implementation timeline extending to mid-2029, citing, among other

 considerations, capacity market alignment and system development needs (see PJM Initial

 Brief). DCC recognizes that certain aspects of the proposed framework may require system

 changes and coordination with existing market constructs. However, PJM has not demonstrated

 that all elements of the proposed services must be deferred for several years, nor has it identified

 opportunities for phased or interim implementation. Given the immediate and growing demand

 for large load interconnection, the Commission should consider whether certain components of

 the framework can be implemented on an accelerated or staged basis to provide near-term

 benefits while longer-term systems are developed.


VIII.   Conclusion

        DCC appreciates the Commission’s leadership in advancing this important proceeding

 and its commitment to enabling the efficient integration of large loads and associated generation

 resources. PJM’s proposal represents a meaningful effort to respond to the Commission’s

 directives, and PJM’s recent stakeholder engagement has provided helpful clarification regarding



                                                  9
 the intended operation of the proposed services. However, those clarifications also highlight

fundamental issues that must be addressed to ensure that the framework is workable in practice.

       As currently structured, the proposal does not fully implement the Commission’s

directives and instead materially narrows key elements of the framework contemplated in the

Show Cause Order. In particular, the proposal fails to preserve the core value proposition of co-

location, unnecessarily restricts the use of Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, does not

accommodate phased development, and relies on operational constructs that remain

insufficiently defined.

       From a customer perspective, co-location is pursued to achieve faster energization and

greater operational predictability. A framework in which customers may still be curtailed despite

bringing sufficient co-located generation, and are unable to utilize available transmission

capacity on an incremental basis, does not provide a commercially viable pathway to achieve

those objectives. Taken together, the proposal effectively eliminates the flexibility the

Commission sought to introduce and replaces it with an “all-or-nothing” structure that delays

load service and discourages efficient co-location arrangements.

       DCC respectfully urges the Commission to require targeted modifications to ensure that

the final framework:

   •   preserves meaningful linkage between co-located load and generation where appropriate;
   •   allows for flexible and incremental service solutions consistent with the Commission’s
       directives;
   •   accommodates phased development and load ramping;
   •   provides greater clarity regarding operational and curtailment parameters; and
   •   can be implemented in a timeframe that supports current and near-term development.




                                                 10
        With these refinements, the Commission can ensure that this proceeding results in a

durable and commercially viable framework that advances both reliability and economic growth,

consistent with the intent of the Show Cause Order.




Respectfully submitted,
